config.title: Climbing Stairs

intro.title: Climbing Stairs
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function to solve the 'Climbing Stairs' lesson, which calculates the number of distinct ways to reach the top of a staircase by taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. You will learn the core programming concept of dynamic programming, which breaks down a complex lesson into simpler overlapping subproblems. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, recursion, and memoization to optimize performance. By the end, you will understand how to implement an efficient solution and apply this approach to similar algorithmic challenges.
intro.usecase: The climbing stairs algorithm pattern appears in dynamic programming scenarios where you need to calculate the number of ways to reach a goal with incremental steps. In real software, this translates to calculating possible combinations in e-commerce checkout flows, determining valid navigation paths through multi-step forms, or computing possible configurations in product customization tools. Developers use this pattern when building progress trackers, step-by-step wizards, or any interface where users make sequential choices with cumulative outcomes. Understanding this algorithm helps optimize performance in features like pricing calculators, workflow builders, or any system requiring efficient combinatorial calculations.

objectives: Implement a recursive solution to calculate the number of ways to climb stairs
Apply memoization to optimize the recursive climbing stairs algorithm
Construct an iterative dynamic programming solution for the climbing stairs lesson
Initialize and manipulate an array to store intermediate results in the dynamic programming approach
Configure the base cases for both recursive and iterative implementations
Integrate the climbing stairs solution into a complete JavaScript function
Control the function flow to handle edge cases like zero or negative input

content.body: You're at the bottom of a staircase with n steps. Each time you can climb 1 or 2 steps. How many distinct ways can you reach the top? Let's discover a clever way to solve this by reusing what we already know.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply the 'reuse smaller solutions' thinking to stair climbing
• Implement a dynamic programming solution in JavaScript
• Explain why storing previous results makes the algorithm efficient
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start small. For 1 step: you can only take 1 step → 1 way. For 2 steps: you can take 1+1 or 2 → 2 ways. What about 3 steps? Think about your first move: take 1 step (then you have 2 left) or take 2 steps (then you have 1 left).
content.title: Try small cases

content.body: For 3 steps: If you start with 1 step, you have 2 steps left (which we know has 2 ways). If you start with 2 steps, you have 1 step left (which has 1 way). So total ways = 2 + 1 = 3. See how we reused answers for 2 and 1 steps?
content.title: Notice the pattern

content.body: Now for 4 steps: First move options? Start with 1 step (3 left → 3 ways) or start with 2 steps (2 left → 2 ways). Total = 3 + 2 = 5. Notice we're adding the previous two results each time.
content.title: Try 4 steps

content.body: You manually calculated ways for small n by breaking the lesson into smaller versions. This is the essence of dynamic programming: solve small lessons first, then build up.
content.title: What you did

content.body: If we tried to calculate ways for 10 steps by brute force, we'd have to explore all 1/2-step combinations. That's exponential! But we noticed we keep solving the same smaller lessons over and over.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Dynamic programming is about 'remembering solved smaller lessons.' Instead of recalculating ways for 3 steps every time we need it, we store the answer and reuse it. This is the 'fill a table' approach: solve from bottom up, avoid doing the same work twice.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Imagine filling a table where each cell stores the number of ways for that many steps. Each new entry just adds the two previous entries.

content.body: We'll create an array (our 'table') where dp[i] = ways to reach step i. Start with dp[1] = 1, dp[2] = 2. For each step from 3 to n: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]. We're reusing the stored answers!
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Handle edge cases (n = 1 or 2)
2. Create array to store results for each step
3. Fill base cases (1 and 2 steps)
4. Loop from step 3 to n, filling each using previous two
5. Return the result for n steps
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function climbStairs that takes n (number of steps) and returns the number of distinct ways.
steps.hint: Just the function signature for now.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure it's a function named climbStairs that takes parameter n.

steps.title: Handle base cases
steps.instruction: First, handle the simple cases: if n is 1 or 2, return n immediately.
steps.hint: Use an if statement to check n === 1 or n === 2.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! These are our base cases.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Don't forget to return the values.

steps.title: Create the table
steps.instruction: Now create an array dp to store results. Initialize it with dp[1] = 1 and dp[2] = 2.
steps.hint: Create an array of size n+1 so indices match step numbers.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there! Remember to set dp[1] and dp[2].
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: let dp = new Array(n + 1); dp[1] = 1; dp[2] = 2;

steps.title: Fill the table
steps.instruction: Loop from i = 3 to n, filling dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]. Then return dp[n].
steps.hint: Use a for loop and remember we already have dp[1] and dp[2].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress! Check your loop condition and the addition formula.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: for (let i = 3; i <= n; i++) { dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]; } then return dp[n];

content.body: Great work! You've solved Climbing Stairs using dynamic programming. Remember: 1) Store solutions to smaller lessons, 2) Build up from base cases, 3) Reuse stored results to avoid redundant work. This 'fill a table' approach makes exponential lessons efficient!
content.title: Done

familyTeachingProfile.conceptBridge: Introduce 'remembering solved smaller lessons'; focus on reuse, not formula memorization.
familyTeachingProfile.visualMetaphor: Fill a table or reuse previous results; avoid doing the same work twice.
commonConfusions: In what order do we solve subproblems?
